why: Worn out; he has to sit a while

journal.text: First proper day ashore, and I'm writing this by firelight with bracken up to my knees. Got the frame of a lean-to up and a ring of stones round the fire, and tonight, God willing, I won't freeze for it. Cut my hand on something in the wreckage this morning — nothing that won't mend. Tired in a way I don't think sleep alone will fix, but the fire's caught and holding, and that's the whole of my luck today and I'll take it. Tomorrow: the roof, before the weather remembers where it left off.

A boat passed this evening, out beyond the reef — the first sign of another living soul since I came ashore. I watched its lights a good while before they went. Didn't call out; it would never have carried, and I hadn't the strength to make a fool of myself for nothing. Belly's empty and won't let me forget it, but the fire's banked and should hold till morning. Next time a boat comes by, I want smoke enough to be seen, not just watched for.

Slept the whole night under a finished roof and didn't once wake shivering — small thing to be proud of, but I'll take my pride where I find it out here. The dog was at the treeline again this morning, close enough to see her properly this time: thin but not starving, watching me the way I watch the tide. Didn't push it. Today I want poles for a signal tripod, dry wood packed in the middle, so if another boat comes by there's more than moonlight to see me by. Belly's still asking questions I can't fully answer yet, but one thing at a time.

A day's proper work behind me and my arms know it. Fish trap's in the water, two snares laid along the warren path, wood stacking up on the rack before the weather turns. Best of it though: I set scraps out for the dog and backed off, and she came and ate them, watching me the whole time like I might change my mind about being harmless. Didn't try to touch her — that's a day for another time. Still just the two of us out here, but it feels a little less like just the one.

Third day, and I made it through a hungry night without it turning into anything worse. Whatever I managed between the trap, the snares and what's left in my hands has quieted my stomach, if not answered every question about tomorrow. Fire's out again — that's twice now, and I'm getting tired of relighting it from scratch each morning. Fog's thick enough I can't see the shore from the lean-to. Feeling the quiet of this place more today than I have — no one to grumble to about any of it but myself, and Nell, who isn't much for conversation yet. Fire first, then the woodpile cover, then I'll see what the fog gives up.

lastThought: Piling leaf litter over the debris hut, arm-deep, and it's coming on well. But that fire's been cold since last night and I keep telling myself I'll see to it after this next handful of leaves. No more excuses — soon as this pile's done.
